question: In the condition known as crocodile tears, through which nerve are ﬁbers originally supplying the mandibular and sublingual glands redirected to the lacrimal gland?
explanation: After any facial neuropathy, but most commonly as a result of Bell palsy, regenerating axons may reinnervate diﬀerent muscles from those originally served; such aberrant regeneration can cause synkinetic movements. Disorders of aberrant facial innervation include lacrimation caused by chewing (crocodile tears), in which ﬁbers originally supplying mandibular and sublingual glands reinnervate the lacrimal gland by way of the greater superﬁcial petrosal nerve. This syndrome usually develops after severe injury to the proximal CN VII and may be accompanied by decreased reﬂex tearing and decreased ability to taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. In another example, when axons originally destined for the orbicularis oculi reinnervate the lower facial muscles, each blink may cause a twitch of the corner of the mouth or a dimpling of the chin. Conversely, movements of the lower face—such as pursing the lips, smiling, or chewing with the mouth closed—may produce involuntary eyelid closure. The supraorbital and supratrochlear nerve branch from the frontal nerve in CN V. The nasociliary nerve is also a branch of CN V.

The headache occurs in 97% of cases; 30% have symptoms lateralized to the side of the hemorrhage. The combination of vitreous hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage (Terson syndrome) portends a worse prognosis. Maintaining a high index of suspicion and evaluating the patient with noncontrast CT, followed by mandatory lumbar puncture if CT results are negative, are essential in making the diagnosis. Terson syndrome is a vitreous and sub-ILM or subhyaloid hemorrhage caused by an abrupt intracranial hemorrhage. Although the exact mechanism is not known, it is suspected that the acute intracranial hemorrhage causes an acute rise in the intraocular venous pressure, resulting in a rupture of peripapillary and retinal vessels. Approximately one-third of patients with subarachnoid or subdural hemorrhage have associated intraocular hemorrhage, which may include intraretinal and subretinal bleeding. question: A 79-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of diﬃculty chewing food, and of weight loss and headache. Her dentist recently diagnosed her with temperomandibular joint (TMJ) inﬂammation and prescribed ibuprofen. Over the past week, she has experienced transient visual loss in the left eye. The ophthalmologic examination is normal except for 1 cotton-wool spot in the left fundus. What is the best next step?

options.A: Evaluate immediately in the emergency department, preferably one associated with a stroke center.
options.B: Check erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) and arrange outpatient follow-up.
options.C: Order computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the neck and echocardiogram as outpatient workup.
options.D: Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and orbits with contrast.

explanation: In a patient of this age with transient monocular visual loss, 2 potentially devastating vascular causes must be evaluated immediately: (1) giant cell arteritis and (2) embolic phenomena. If an embolic cause is suspected, then a complete vascular and cardiac work up must proceed urgently, due to the increased risk of morbidity and mortality from stroke in this setting. Giant cell arteritis must also be ruled out in patients over age 50. Embolic evaluation must include (1) imaging of the carotid arteries (with Doppler, MRA, or CTA), (2) MRI with diﬀusion weighted imaging (DWI) to evaluate for associated cerebral ischemia, and (3) echocardiography to evaluate for valvular and cardiac wall defects, intracardiac tumors, and large thrombi. If a cardiac or carotid source for embolism is not found, then other systemic processes that could contribute to stroke must also be considered, including advanced age, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, and sleep apnea.

question: A 75-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to clinic after an episode of transient monocular vision loss, characterized by acute, painless vision loss in the right eye only, preceded by a descending curtain over the vision, which then resolved over 10 minutes. The episode occurred earlier that morning. Ocular examination is unremarkable. What is the best next step in management?

options.C: magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.D: lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal ﬂuid studies

explanation: This patient has a classic presentation of typical demyelinating optic neuritis, which is characterized by a subacute or acute unilateral visual loss associated with pain with eye movements, moderately decreased visual acuity with severe dyschromatopsia, and visual ﬁeld loss (central scotoma in this case). The fundus is normal in approximately two-thirds of cases, with one-third of cases having optic nerve edema (anterior optic neuritis or papillitis). While lumbar puncture and serologic testing may be helpful for atypical optic neuritis presentations and for helping to diagnose multiple sclerosis (MS), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain should be performed in every case of typical optic neuritis to assess the long-term risk for developing MS over the next 15 years (25% if no lesions, 72% with ≥ 1 lesion). Treatment with Intravenous steroids may be useful for decreasing the risk of conversion to MS in isolated optic neuritis as well as improving recovery time, but it is not a necessary next step in management of optic neuritis.

question: A 29-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of right eye pain and blurred vision. Her best-corrected visual acuity is 20/50 in the right eye and 20/15 in the left eye. There is a right relative aﬀerent pupillary defect (RAPD). Her color vision is 1/14 in the right eye and 14/14 in the left eye. Her right optic nerve and right visual ﬁeld are shown below. explanation: This scenario describes right V (decreased corneal sensation), VI (esotropia worse on right gaze), VII (lagophthalmos), and possibly VIII cranial nerve palsies (dizziness) in combination. CPA tumors, especially acoustic neuroma or meningioma, can cause V, VI, VII, and/or VIII nerve palsies with the above ﬁndings, as well as ipsilateral decreased hearing. question: A 79-year-old woman presents with an acute onset of binocular horizontal diplopia and dizziness. Examination reveals a right head turn with an esotropia that is worse on right gaze. There is decreased corneal sensation and lagophthalmos on the right. What is the location of the lesion? &

options.A: sixth-nerve palsy with spread of comitance

explanation: New-onset diplopia in an adult can result from muscular, neuromuscular, or neurological causes. This patient has full ductions and no constitutional symptoms, such as weakness or headache. Her manifest strabismus is comitant. Comitant misalignment characteristically is found in patients with congenital or early-onset strabismus. Patients with this condition do not typically report diplopia, because there is suppression of the image from one eye. However, they may develop diplopia later in life. For instance, patients with a long-standing exophoria may develop diplopia in their ﬁfth decade of life, when convergence and accommodative capacities decrease. While there can be a spread of comitance with a sixth-nerve palsy, it does not occur within just a few weeks. She has no other symptoms to suggest increased intracranial pressure. Convergence spasm would not produce constant double vision for 3 weeks and would not produce a comitant misalignment, but it would give a larger-angle strabismus in lateral gazes.

question: Three weeks ago, a 49-year-old woman developed constant diplopia. She feels well and reports no new headache, fatigue, numbness, or weakness. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU, with equal pupils. Ductions are normal, and at distance there is a 15 PD exotropia in all positions of gaze. Stereopsis is poor even with prism correction. What is the most likely cause of her diplopia?
explanation: The third-order sympathetic ﬁbers to the orbit enter the intracranial space with the internal carotid artery, and then travel brieﬂy on the sixth nerve within the cavernous sinus, before joining the third nerve ﬁbers destined for the pupil. Also, pontine lesions can produce a Horner syndrome (aﬀecting the ﬁrst-order neuron of the sympathetic pathway) associated with an ipsilateral abducens nerve paresis. In no other anatomic location are the sixth nerve and sympathetic ﬁbers in close enough proximity to result in Horner syndrome and an ipsilateral sixth nerve palsy without other BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the most likely site of a lesion causing an ipsilateral sixth nerve palsy and Horner syndrome?
explanation: This prompt describes convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, a ﬁnding in dorsal midbrain syndrome (also termed pretectal syndrome or Parinaud syndrome). Dorsal midbrain syndrome is caused by compression of the posterior commissure, which controls horizontal conjugate eye movements. It includes any of the following ﬁndings: conjugate limitation of vertical gaze (usually upgaze), convergence- retraction nystagmus, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation, lid retraction in primary position, skew deviation, convergence spasm or palsy, and increased square-wave jerks. Given the papilledema with enlarged blind spots bilaterally, there is likely increased intracranial pressure from a mass or hydrocephalus compressing the dorsal midbrain at the level of the pineal gland, associated with cerebral aqueductal stenosis. Periventricular white-matter lesions are often seen in multiple sclerosis. Demyelination from multiple sclerosis can produce dorsal midbrain syndrome but would not cause papilledema and signs of increased intracranial pressure demonstrated in this case. Transverse sinus thrombosis could cause increased intracranial pressure and papilledema but would not cause dorsal midbrain syndrome. Occlusion of the vertebrobasilar artery that supplies the pretectum could cause dorsal midbrain syndrome, but it is not associated with increased intracranial pressure.

question: A 23-year-old woman has headache and bilateral optic disc swelling. She takes daily efavirenz, lamivudine/zidovudine, and oral contraceptives. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of her brain shows diﬀuse leptomeningeal enhancement without any evidence of intracranial mass. The cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) specimen is shown in Figure 1. What is her diagnosis? &
explanation: The possibility of an aneurysm at the origin of the posterior communicating artery from the internal carotid artery must be urgently evaluated in a patient presenting with a new-onset painful pupil-involving third cranial nerve palsy. Saccular (“berry”) aneurysms are the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and the origin of the posterior communicating artery is a frequently involved site. Intracerebral hemorrhage, which is most commonly due to hypertension, can present with focal neurologic symptoms but a pupil-sparing third cranial nerve palsy would be atypical. Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) can cause intracerebral hemorrhage as well as SAH. When associated with SAH, AVMs may manifest with focal seizures, progressive worsening of focal neurologic signs, and recurrent unilateral migraine-like headache. Intraventricular hemorrhage usually occurs as a secondary phenomenon in patients with an intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage. It typically manifests with sudden-onset headache, nausea, vomiting, and varying degrees of impaired consciousness. Microvascular ischemia to the third cranial nerve can also cause sudden-onset pain, ptosis, and partial ophthalmoplegia, but pupil involvement is generally mild (less than 1 mm of anisocoria).
